title: Sweat like drops of blood (Luke 22:39–46)
hookLine: on the Mount of Olives an angel strengthens him

cards: After the supper, Luke says, Jesus went out to the Mount of Olives, as he usually did. This is his place; he's been sleeping out here all week.

The disciples follow him in the dark, and he tells them to pray that they don't enter into temptation. Then he walks away from them, about a stone's throw, and kneels down. Close enough to hear, far enough to be alone.
If you've ever stepped out of a hospital waiting room to stand in a hallway by yourself, you know that distance.

teach.b: He prays, in the King James words: "Father, if thou be willing, remove this cup from me: nevertheless not my will, but thine, be done." The cup, in the Hebrew Bible, can be a picture of suffering poured out.
He asks, honestly, not to drink it, then hands the answer back.
Then two verses only Luke has. "And there appeared an angel unto him from heaven, strengthening him." The angel doesn't take the cup away, and doesn't explain anything.

teach.h: AN ANGEL GIVES STRENGTH, NOT ESCAPE.
teach.b: It gives him strength to go through. "And being in an agony he prayed more earnestly: and his sweat was as it were great drops of blood falling down to the ground." As it were: Luke is making a comparison.
Some readers take it literally, pointing to a rare condition where extreme stress can bring blood into sweat. Others read it as a picture of how heavy the sweat fell. The text allows both.
Agony, in Greek, was first a word for a contest, a wrestling match. Here he's wrestling in prayer.

teach.h: AN ANGEL UNTO HIM, STRENGTHENING HIM.
teach.b: One honest note: these two verses are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts of Luke, and present in others.
Scholars still debate whether they were original, and Christians have read and loved them for many centuries.
When he gets up, he finds the disciples asleep, and Luke gently gives the reason: they were sleeping for sorrow.

how: Christians remember the agony in the garden on Maundy Thursday night, often by keeping watch in prayer for an hour, and Catholics pray it as the first sorrowful mystery of the rosary.

o: a deep sorrow for the wrong you've done
a struggle or contest, like a wrestler's strain
a sudden fear that freezes you in place

games.q: what's inside Luke 22:39–46 — tap the pairs.
p: where he went, as he usually did
how far he went to pray

s: the angel takes the cup away from Jesus
the angel strengthens him to go through it.
Luke says the sweat was 'as it were' great drops of blood
a comparison; some read it literally, some as a picture.
the verses about the angel and the sweat appear in every ancient manuscript
they are missing from some of the oldest manuscripts of Luke and present in others.

games.q: you're kneeling alone, facing what you dread most. you've asked for it to pass. what comes?
o: an angel comes and strengthens you.
games.why: "there appeared an angel unto him from heaven, strengthening him." not escape: strength to go through.

practice: Think of one hard thing you can't avoid: a conversation, a diagnosis, a long week, a grief. Say honestly that you wish it would go away; Jesus said it too.

Then shift the ask from take this from me to help me go through it, and if you pray, ask God for that strength; if you don't, notice where your own strength is, in your breath, your feet, the people near you.

wordCard.voice: Agonia, the Greek word for a struggle, an athlete's strain, the source of agony: Luke's picture of Jesus's prayer on the Mount of Olives, when he asked for the cup to pass and an angel came to strengthen him.

orig.note: Greek: a contest, a struggle, an athlete's strain before a match. the source of the English word agony.

carryVoice: Your line: an angel strengthened him. Strength to go through, not a way around. Day five hundred eighty, done.
